Supplementary material for: Choosing an analysis for clustered binary outcomes when clusters are few and series are short: a simulation study and two clinical applications

This supplement accompanies the manuscript. Every number is read from the same registry of values as the main text. GB = GenBinaryY, NAT = GLMM-native, AR1 = GLMM-AR1, COP = Copula-AR1; MMM = marginalized multilevel model. In every table the Kauermann-Carroll correction is computed with fewclust (Section S4). Numbers in square brackets refer to the reference list of the main text.

Scenarios and mechanisms not in the table use the same code. M1c has the mean model of M1 with the prevalence (0.59) and between-subject variance (3.5) of the clinical cohort. M6 and M7 let the latent standard deviation of GenBinaryY grow by 0.1 or 0.25 per occasion, and give GLMM-native a random-slope variance of 0.01 or 0.04. Copula-AR1 has the marginal coefficients of each scenario and latent correlation ρ = 0.6 (Section S8). Covariates are drawn as follows: age, per subject, rnorm(n = N, mean = 50, sd = 10), then standardized; dose, per observation, rnorm(n = length(id)), then standardized; steroids, per subject, sample(x = 1:3, size = N, replace = TRUE), in the transition model of GenBinaryY M5 only. Treatment is rbinom(n = N, size = 1, prob = 0.5) per subject.

The conditional coefficients of GLMM-AR1 are calibrated on each replicate, so that the implied marginal coefficients equal the target. In M6 and M7, with 10 occasions the latent standard deviation of GenBinaryY grows from 1 to 1.9 or 3.25, against 1.09 in M3. The autoregressive parameters of GLMM-AR1 add a serial dependence to the cluster effect. In 44 design points of the main grid and 6 of M1c, all in GLMM-AR1, only 971 to 999 datasets could be generated, because the per-replicate calibration encountered a singular system; every replicate that could not be generated had a degenerate design, defined in Section 2.2 of the main text.

S2. Software

Table S2. Versions in the project library and, for fewclust, in a separate library built from the commit shown, used for every rerun and for the tables of this paper. The simulations were first run under an earlier patch release of R; their datasets were reproduced bit for bit under the current release. The full sessionInfo() is provided with the code (reports/morris/S8b_logs/sessionInfo.txt, with fewclust and clubSandwich loaded). The marginalized model used 20 Gauss-Hermite points; Bie et al. used more with large random-effect variances (reference [19] of the main text), and more points were not examined.

Replicates were run in parallel, each from its own seed, so that any dataset can be regenerated alone; with the L’Ecuyer-CMRG generator the sequences started from different seeds do not overlap in practice, and separate streams [21] were not used. The 2,376 design points comprise 4,752,000 datasets, analysed with about 52.1 million model fits over all runs (a likelihood-ratio test counted once; the logistic fits of the sign-flip test and of its interval search not counted), and every analysis added after the main run regenerated them from their seeds.

S3. Tables of the main grid

The marginalized model without the check is reported as a sensitivity analysis (Table S3). Fits that returned with warnings were kept; excluding them is a sensitivity analysis (Table S13). Counts of miscalibrated cells used exact binomial tests with the Benjamini-Hochberg and Benjamini-Yekutieli corrections.

With the Benjamini-Hochberg correction within method, the marginalized model was detectably off nominal in 1% of its cells, Fay-Graubard in 23%, Mancl-DeRouen in 28% and Kauermann-Carroll in 38% (Table S5). The uncorrected GEE was above 7.5% by 20 points at N = 10 on GenBinaryY. Its smallest excess over 5% across cluster counts was under half a point on every mechanism. Above 45 clusters, Fay-Graubard and the marginalized model were both within about half a point of 5% on the random-effects mechanisms. The ordering of the methods was stable across mechanisms, with Spearman correlations of 0.83 to 0.98 between pairs of mechanisms. GLMM-AR1 differed from GLMM-native by 0.16 percentage points on average across methods.

Section 3.5 of the main text compares Fay-Graubard with exchangeable, independence and AR(1) working correlations over the three study mechanisms. Per design point, 90% of the differences lay between -1.4 and 0.40 points, and 18 of the 1,896 differences with independence and 11 with AR(1) exceeded 2.5 points in absolute value (at most 5.1 and 3.7).

The size-adjusted critical value was the 95th percentile of |estimate/SE| over the usable null replicates of the same cell; for the likelihood-ratio test it was the 5th percentile of the null p-values. It uses the null distribution of each design point, unknown in practice, and serves only to compare methods at equal level. Table S10 gives raw and size-adjusted power. After size adjustment, power ranged from 22% to 27% across methods and mechanisms. On GenBinaryY the Wald test of the mixed model had more size-adjusted power than Fay-Graubard, by 3.3 points with the default optimizer of lme4 and by 3.7 points with the optimizer bobyqa (Section S15). On GLMM-AR1 the difference was about two points with the default optimizer, and the two were similar with bobyqa. On GLMM-native the two were similar with the default optimizer, and with bobyqa Fay-Graubard had more power, by about two points. Part of the size-adjusted power of the Wald test of the mixed model came from fits with a collapsed standard error (\(|\hat\beta/\mathrm{SE}| > 37\), a p-value numerically zero), which the usability limits keep: averaged over the 1,254 cells of the main grid with a size-adjusted value, they made up 2.3 of its 24 percentage points, and in 193 cells the size-adjusted critical value itself exceeded 37.

S4. Numerical behaviour of the small-sample corrections

The corrections of Mancl and DeRouen, Kauermann and Carroll and Fay and Graubard were computed with two implementations. geesmv was used for the exchangeable working correlation. On sparse binary data with few clusters its three functions can loop indefinitely in compiled code, so each call ran in a separate process killed after 5 seconds; the largest share of time-outs at a design point under one hypothesis was 20%. geesmv also takes the clusters from any column named id, whatever cluster variable is passed: in the simulations and in the cohort the cluster column has that name, and in the respiratory trial it was renamed before every call. With AR(1) working correlation geesmv fails as soon as one subject has a single observation, so it was not used with that correlation.

fewclust (Table S2) computes the three corrections from the estimating-equation building blocks. On 666 or more datasets for each working correlation and correction on which both computations returned a standard error, its standard errors agreed with a computation by hand; the largest difference over the three corrections was below \(10^{-12}\). Against geesmv on the same exchangeable fits of the first 50 replicates of each design point and hypothesis, the subsample on which geesmv was run in this comparison (174,804 datasets), Mancl-DeRouen and Fay-Graubard agreed to within one per cent in 98% and 97% of datasets, and Kauermann-Carroll in only 2.0%. geesmv::GEE.var.kc rebuilds \((I - H_{ii})^{-1/2}\) with the transpose of the eigenvectors of a non-symmetric matrix, an identity that holds only for symmetric matrices. With the published formula, Kauermann-Carroll with exchangeable correlation and a t reference had a mean type I error of 5.6% over the 1,896 design points of the three study mechanisms, against 9.7% with geesmv, and it was clearly above 7.5% at 146 instead of 963 design points. With geesmv the correction appears to shrink rather than inflate the variance; this is a property of the implementation, not of the estimator. The CR2 estimator of clubSandwich is the Bell-McCaffrey version of Kauermann-Carroll; it was used here with a t reference on N - p degrees of freedom, not with the Satterthwaite-type degrees of freedom for which it was proposed (reference [27] of the main text), and with those its results could differ.

With exchangeable correlation, Mancl-DeRouen and Fay-Graubard were also computed with geesmv, under a hard time limit of 5 seconds; a time-out counted as an unusable fit, and these values enter Table 3, Table 4 and Table S10. Every Kauermann-Carroll result is from fewclust, because geesmv applies a symmetric matrix square root to a non-symmetric matrix (above). Computed with fewclust instead of geesmv, Fay-Graubard with exchangeable correlation rejected a true null at similar rates (difference 0.061 points) and had a similar usable share (difference 0.21 points). The Kauermann-Carroll correction computed from its published formula rejected a true null 4.1 points less often than the geesmv version on average under a t reference. Its rejection rates in Table 3 and Table S10 are therefore lower than those obtained with geesmv.

S5. Tables of the scenario anchored to the cohort (M1c)

In scenario M1c, the size-adjusted power of the Wald test of the mixed model fell below that of Fay-Graubard, by 4.1 to 4.8 points with the default optimizer. With bobyqa the deficit was about two points on GenBinaryY and GLMM-AR1, and the two were similar on GLMM-native. The default optimizer returned degenerate fits with a near-zero standard error. In M1c, the method with the fewest miscalibrated cells could not be identified.

S6. Degrees of freedom of the t reference

Degrees of freedom N - 2, as used by Li and Redden [15], were examined as a sensitivity analysis. Averaging the Mancl-DeRouen and Kauermann-Carroll variances, as studied by Ford and Westgate [13], did not give a strategy that was never clearly above 7.5%. With N - p degrees of freedom, GEE with AR(1) working correlation and the averaged variance was clearly above 7.5% at 56 of the 2,376 design points of the four mechanisms, and GEE with exchangeable working correlation and the averaged variance at 121 (Table S26 gives the three study mechanisms).

S7. Sign-flip score test and the interval obtained by inverting it

The model without the interaction was fitted as a logistic regression with the mean model of the scenario, and the effective score contribution of each subject to the interaction was obtained by projecting out the other coefficients. The p-value compares the observed sum of contributions with its distribution under random changes of sign: all sign assignments up to 12 subjects, and otherwise 1,999 random assignments plus the identity. The test gives a p-value only; the interval obtained by inverting it is described below.

The sign-flip test of the main text tests the null of no interaction. Testing instead the null that the interaction equals a value \(b_0\), by entering \(b_0 \cdot t \cdot \mathrm{trt}\) as an offset in the model without the interaction, and collecting the values that are not rejected at 5%, gives a confidence interval. Its ends were searched from the independence GEE estimate by a walk in fixed steps followed by bisection, with the same sign vectors at every value and every fit started from the default initial value; a value at which the test was not computable counted as not rejected, so the interval can be unbounded. Under the alternative the test evaluated at the true value kept its level: it covered the true value in 95% of datasets over the 2,376 design points, and its non-coverage was clearly outside Bradley’s band at no design point. The interval, which counts as covering when it is unbounded, covered the true value in 95% of datasets, against 96% for GEE with AR(1) working correlation, Fay-Graubard and a t reference; its non-coverage was clearly below 2.5% at 97 design points under the alternative and 112 under the null, 90 of the former with two occasions, where it is almost always unbounded. Both ends were finite in 79% of datasets, and in 14% with two or three occasions and at most 25 clusters (Table S27). Where both intervals were finite it was wider than the GEE interval by 17% on average over design points (geometric mean of the ratio of widths at each design point, then over design points), and by 6.4% with 75 clusters or more; over datasets, which gives more weight to the larger designs, the geometric mean was 8.7% (5.6% with 75 clusters or more).

With the rules of Section 2.4 of the main text the test was not computable in some of the small designs, often because one arm had only zero outcomes. With two or three occasions and at most 25 clusters it answered in 72% of datasets, against 99.9% when the rules were not applied, with a mean type I error of 5.2%. A version that also excluded fits with a coefficient of at least 10 is a sensitivity analysis. With this coefficient filter, on the 1,896 design points of the three study mechanisms, it rejected a true null in 5.5% of datasets on average, was clearly above 7.5% at 0 design points and answered in 97% of datasets.

S8. The fourth mechanism

Copula-AR1 draws, for each subject, a vector of normal scores with correlation \(\rho^{|t_j - t_k|}\) (ρ = 0.6) and sets each outcome to one when its score is below the normal quantile of the marginal mean of the scenario. The marginal means are therefore exactly those of the scenario, and the correlation between occasions of a subject decreases with their distance in time, with no component that is constant within subject. Without the convergence check the marginalized model was clearly above 7.5% at 62 of the 480 design points. To check whether the excess of the mixed model comes from a non-zero null value of its conditional coefficient, a single dataset of 20,000 subjects was generated under the null for T = 2, 4 and 10 and fitted with a random intercept: the estimates ranged from 0.0046 to 0.060, with standard errors up to 0.12, none distinguishable from zero. On the latent scale the correlation of Copula-AR1 is that of the AR(1) working correlation of Section 2.4 of the main text; on the binary outcomes it was 0.36 between adjacent occasions and 0.20 two occasions apart, so it decays more slowly than an AR(1) correlation with the same first-lag value. The fourth mechanism was simulated on the main grid only, with the seeds of the other three.

With a random intercept only, and N ≥ 85, under the null and averaged over the design points of each scenario and number of occasions, the model-based standard error of the mixed model (root mean square over replicates) was 0.64 to 0.81 times the standard deviation of its estimates, while the estimates were centred. The marginalized model estimated the interaction with a mean bias of 0.026 empirical standard errors and covered the true value in 94% of replicates under a normal reference, although its model of the dependence is misspecified on this mechanism (Table S28).

S9. Second clinical application: the respiratory trial

The respiratory trial distributed with geepack has 111 patients observed at four visits. The full mean model had treatment, baseline status, visit, age, sex and centre; the reduced model had treatment and baseline status only. Kauermann-Carroll was computed with fewclust on the same GEE fits and the same draws, in both applications; Mancl-DeRouen and Fay-Graubard were computed with geesmv. Recomputed with fewclust, these two agreed with geesmv to within one per cent in 99% and 99% of the draws of the cohort and in 99.9% and 99.6% of those of the trial. In both applications the marginalized model had a latent variable with an intercept only (20 quadrature points) and the main text reports its model-based standard error. With its robust standard error the corrected ratio of Section 2.7 of the main text was 0.85 to 0.99 in the cohort and 0.55 to 0.87 in the trial; on the full data the robust standard error was 0.17 in the cohort and 0.35 in the trial. In the respiratory trial the contrast of interest was the treatment effect, adjusted for baseline status, visit, age, sex and centre; the latent variable of the marginalized model had an intercept only, as in the cohort, since with four visits per patient a time trend of the latent standard deviation would rest on four observations per patient.

In the trial, the bias of the marginalized model against its full-data estimate was within two Monte Carlo standard errors of zero at 10 and at 50 patients and reached 0.40 at 15 (Table S30). Its corrected ratio, with the model-based standard error, was 0.70 at 10 patients and 0.85 at 50.

S10. The marginalized model and the GEE strategy compared

The strategy selected by the decision rule, the marginalized model with the convergence check, was compared with the GEE strategy (AR(1) working correlation, Fay-Graubard correction) by number of clusters and of occasions after the results had been seen, both with a t reference, with the block bootstrap and the one-point margin for mean differences of Section 2.5 of the main text. The marginalized model was never clearly above 7.5%; the GEE strategy was clearly above 7.5% at 2 design points, both with ten clusters and two occasions (Section 3.4 of the main text). Before the datasets with a constant outcome were excluded (Section 2.5 of the main text), the GEE strategy was usable in 172 and 136 replicates at these two design points, with the same 12 and 11 rejections: every excluded dataset had been a usable non-rejection, so the exclusion raised the rate. The comparison does not enter the rule (Table 5). With two or three occasions and at most 25 clusters the GEE strategy returned a usable result more often, by 16 points.

S11. What the decision rule guarantees

The rule replaces a criterion that selected at each cluster count the method with the highest unconditional validity, and was fixed after the results of the version that used that criterion had been seen (Section 4.1 of the main text).

A design point is clearly above 7.5% when the lower limit of the exact 95% interval of its rejection rate exceeds 7.5%. With 1,000 usable replicates this requires an observed rate of at least 9.3%, with half as many 10%, and with a tenth as many 14%. A strategy that is never clearly above 7.5% is therefore one in which no excess was detected. Table S32 gives, for every strategy of Table 5, the design points at which an excess could not be excluded (upper limit of the exact interval above 7.5%, but not clearly above) and the highest rate observed. An exact interval was used because with no rejections the binomial Monte Carlo standard error is zero. The highest rate at a design point was 20% for the GEE strategy and 8.5% for the marginalized model, and an excess could not be excluded, the upper limit of the exact interval lying above 7.5%, at 227 and 402 design points (Table S32).

Its two design points with the published limit therefore depend on datasets with an estimate or a standard error between 5 and 10 in absolute value.

S12. Adaptive quadrature for the mixed model

This analysis was added after the main run. The mixed model with a random intercept (scenarios M1, M2 and M1c) was refitted with lme4::glmer and nAGQ = 10 on the same null datasets, at 123 design points: N ∈ {10, 25, 55, 145} and T ∈ {2, 4, 10} in M1 and M2 on the four mechanisms, and N ∈ {10, 25, 45} and T ∈ {2, 4, 6} in M1c on the three study mechanisms. Only the number of quadrature nodes changed; formula, optimizer and usability limits were those of the study. Refitted by the Laplace approximation, the 122,904 replicate fits reproduced the stored estimates and standard errors exactly. On the first 100 replicates of each design point the fit was repeated with 25 nodes, which gave a different decision in 10 of the 9,844 fits usable for both. Quadrature lowered the rejection rate most at two occasions with 145 clusters, from 10% to 20% under the Laplace approximation to 2.6% to 4.5%.

S13. Estimation by the marginalized model with the check in scenarios M6-M7

In M6-M7 the fit that the convergence check substitutes, without a time trend of the latent standard deviation, is misspecified. Table S35 gives bias, standard error and coverage of the marginalized model with the check against the marginal true value, and the same coverage and standard-error ratio separately for usable fits that are the fit without the time trend and for those that are the original fit; a fit at the boundary whose refit did not converge gives no usable result (Section 2.4 of the main text). Intervention depends on the data, so the split is a description, not a criterion. The estimates of the marginalized model with the check had a bias of at most 0.55 empirical standard errors at any design point, its model-based standard error, averaged over replicates, was a median 2.0% to 4.2% below the empirical one across scenarios and hypotheses, and the t interval covered the true value in 95% to 96% of replicates on average, with non-coverage clearly above 7.5% at no design point (Table S35). Usable fits that are the fit without the time trend covered the true value as often as the others (Table S35). Under a normal reference its mean type I error was 5.2% to 5.8% across the four scenarios. GEE with exchangeable working correlation and Fay-Graubard with a t reference was clearly above 7.5% at 4 design points, 3 of them on GenBinaryY with the steeper slope (M7) (Table 5 and Figure S1).

S14. Previous evaluations of the small-sample corrections

Cluster-randomized trials with ten to thirty clusters are common. Among 100 reviewed trials, the 99 that reported the number of clusters had a median of 25 (interquartile range 15 to 44) [5], and Barker et al., citing an earlier review, reported that 45% of stepped-wedge trials had fewer than ten clusters [6]. In the evaluations cited here, the unit within a cluster is a site within a mouth [7], a patient within a general practice [9], a participant within a cluster [15,19] or a youth within a community [20]. None is a subject measured on several occasions. Cluster sizes range from 4 observations per cluster [20] to 150 on average [15].

Three results are established elsewhere and are cited rather than claimed here: the uncorrected sandwich is anticonservative with few clusters [7,8], the corrections trade level for power [15,17], and marginal and conditional estimands differ [4].

S15. Further details of the methods and performance measures

For the likelihood-ratio test, both nested fits had to return and the p-value had to be finite. Its full fit used the optimizer bobyqa in both stages with a limit of \(10^5\) function evaluations, whereas the Wald test used the default of lme4 2.0.6 (bobyqa, then Nelder-Mead); the Wald test of that full fit is reported as the mixed model with bobyqa (Section S3 and Section S5).

The Wald statistic of the shrinkage GLM equals that of the mixed model on the same fit; its rejection rate can still differ, because the usability limits of Section 2.5 of the main text apply to the rescaled estimate and standard error.

In the block bootstrap of the direct comparison of the two strategies of the rule (Table S31), scenario M1c, whose seeds are those of M1, was resampled with its own indices rather than jointly with M1; this affects only the Monte Carlo standard errors of that comparison.

In the text, values are given to two significant figures, or fewer where the MCSE does not support them. Tables give the digit that the MCSE supports, with the MCSE in the caption.

S16. The convergence check of the marginalized model: diagnosis and sensitivity analyses

MMLB::mm writes the latent standard deviation with an exponentiated slope, so a slope near zero lies on the boundary of the parameter space, and in scenarios M3-M5 the generating slope was close to zero. At the boundary nlm either stopped without converging or converged with a collapsed standard error. Both failures produced excess rejections that grew with the number of occasions. This is why, without the check, the marginalized model appears miscalibrated with long series.

The check was specified after the diagnosis and before the reanalysis of the 1,685,204 fits of M3-M5 that returned an estimate. The check changed raw power at eight or ten occasions by 0.26 points on average.

Thresholds of 0.0001 and 0.01 were examined as sensitivity analyses, and scenarios M6-M7 were simulated afterwards to test the check. With the thresholds 0.0001 and 0.01 in place of 0.001, and the same rules for the refit and for constant outcomes, the tables were recomputed from the stored fits. The reading (difference, similar or about the margin; Section 2.5 of the main text) changed in 0 and 0 of the 156 comparisons of the claim table of the main grid; of the 37 cited in this paper, 0 and 0 changed. With either threshold, the marginalized model with a t reference was clearly above 7.5% at 0 and 0 design points of the main grid and M1c.

S17. The neonatal cohort: subsampling details

Subsampling whole patients preserves the dependence structure exactly, and the covariate distribution only in expectation. Of the 25 patients ventilated invasively, a draw of 10 contains none with probability 0.27, and the mean model is then not identifiable.

In subsamples of 10 patients, 22% of draws contained no invasively ventilated patient (expected proportion 0.27 under the simple random draws of Section 2.7 of the main text, a deviation of 2.5 binomial standard errors at this size and of at most 1.1 at the others), so that the mean model could not be fitted (Table S15). Among the fits that were returned, a usable result was obtained by the mixed model in 100%, by the marginalized model in 100% and by the uncorrected GEE in 92%. It was obtained by Fay-Graubard in 45% and by Mancl-DeRouen in 20%; most failures of the corrections returned a point estimate without a standard error.

Section 3.11 of the main text reports, for the mixed model in the cohort, the ratio of its model-based standard error to the empirical standard deviation of its estimates. A random intercept for the patient-timepoint did not change this ratio (0.50 to 0.57), because its variance was estimated at the boundary in the subsamples. The posterior-versus-anterior contrast varied strongly between patients, which a random intercept ignores: with a random slope for posterior zones (variance 10 in the full cohort) the ratio rose to 0.66 to 0.73 at 25 patients or more, so this heterogeneity explains part of the shortfall.

The bias of the marginalized model against its full-cohort estimate fell from 0.17 at 10 patients to a value within two Monte Carlo standard errors of zero at 50.

S19. Separated datasets

In a separated dataset a linear combination of the covariates of the mean model predicts the outcome perfectly, so the maximum likelihood estimate of the logistic mean model does not exist [31]. Every dataset with an estimable design and a non-constant outcome was regenerated from its seed and checked by linear programming [32] with the mean model of the GEEs (time, treatment and their interaction, plus age in M2 and dose in M5); the R package detectseparation [33] identified which coefficients had infinite estimates. On a stratified sample of 9,504 datasets the linear-programming check written for the study and detectseparation agreed on every dataset.

Of the 4,739,647 datasets with an estimable design and a non-constant outcome, 357,701 were separated (7.5%): 55% of those with two or three occasions and at most 25 clusters, and 0.98% of those with 45 clusters or more. In 357,545 the estimate of the interaction itself was infinite. The usability limit of Section 2.5 of the main text does not identify these datasets: in the sample, an ordinary logistic regression gave an interaction above 10 in absolute value in 503 of the 729 separated datasets, so the limit removed only part of them.

The primary analysis keeps separated datasets and judges each method’s result on them by the usability rule (Section 2.5 of the main text). Over all design points, 0.19% of the usable results of the GEE strategy came from datasets with an infinite interaction, against 4 of the 4,014,389 usable results of the marginalized model with the check. At the two design points where the GEE strategy was clearly above 7.5% (M2, N = 10, T = 2; GLMM-AR1 and GLMM-native), it rejected a true null in 12 of 61 and 11 of 63 usable replicates; 12 and 11 of these rejections were on datasets with an infinite interaction, which were 27 and 26 of its usable replicates. Refitting these separated datasets with 200 instead of the 25 iterations of the study moved the GEE estimate further from zero, by more than 0.5 on the logit scale, in 35 of 53.

Table S38 repeats the rule of Table 5 with separated datasets removed from the usable results, in four sensitivity versions with unchanged denominators: (a) datasets with an infinite interaction removed for the strategies with a Wald interval (GEEs, marginalized model, Wald test of the mixed model, shrinkage GLM); (b) the same datasets removed for every strategy, including the likelihood-ratio and sign-flip tests; (c) every separated dataset removed for the strategies with a Wald interval; (d) as (a), plus the datasets in which the outcome varies within at most one subject, all events or all non-events fall in one subject, one arm has no events or only events, or one arm has a single subject observed after the first occasion. In every version the GEE strategy is no longer clearly above 7.5% at any design point and, answering more often, is the strategy the rule selects; the marginalized model with the check is selected only in the primary analysis.

In the clinical applications, an infinite treatment contrast occurred in 365 of the 5,000 subsamples of the respiratory trial and in 0 subsamples of the cohort.

S20. Versions of the convergence check

The check declares a fit of the marginalized model at the boundary when nlm does not report convergence (return code other than 1 or 2) or an estimated slope of the latent standard deviation is below 0.001 (Section 2.4 of the main text). The primary analysis replaces such a fit by the fit without the time trend only when nlm reports convergence for that refit and its estimate and standard error are finite; otherwise the dataset gives no usable result. Under the null, the check declared 71% of the fits of M3-M5 at the boundary on the main grid, 45% in M6-M7 and 76% on the fourth mechanism, and left 16%, 8.2% and 16% without a result.

Table S39 compares the primary rule with four other versions, computed on the same stored fits by a script written independently of the pipeline of the tables; for version (iii) it reproduces Table 5. Keeping the original fit when the refit does not converge, version (ii), leaves the marginalized model clearly above 7.5% at 4 design points, so that no strategy with an interval would meet the rule. Accepting a refit that did not converge, version (i), which an earlier version of this analysis used, raises the usable share to 91%.
